title: Nayack (Fort Hamilton)
summary: Nayack is connected with the New Utrecht point of land at present-day Fort Hamilton, directly opposite Staten Island. The history preserves a western Long Island shore name tied to the Narrows and the New Netherland period.
map_geometry_source: approximate modern Fort Hamilton marker for Nayack point; not exact historical boundary
ancestral_territory_note: Shown in relation to Canarsie Traditional Land on the current ancestral territory map.
why_this_matters: Danckaerts’ 1679 visit shows Nayack families farming, cooking and working on a corner of land they had to rent back from the man who bought it.
introduction_content:
Nayack was a Lenape community at today’s Fort Hamilton, beside the Narrows. People living there were known by their home place, as Nayack.

Robert S. Grumet, New World Encounters: Jasper Danckaerts’ View of Indian Life in 17th-Century Brooklyn (Brooklyn: The Brooklyn Historical Society, 1986), exhibition catalog: Brooklyn place identities, archaeology, Danckaerts’ observations, “The Brooklyn Indian Diaspora” and Brooklyn’s Native community.
history_content:
Nayack belongs to the western Long Island shoreline at New Utrecht and Fort Hamilton. Dated New Netherland context appear in the Historic Timeline.

A Najack longhouse in 1679

On September 30, 1679, Jasper Danckaerts walked along the shore and “came to the plantation of the Najack Indians, which was planted with maize.” An old woman, about eighty, was beating beans from their pods. Seven or eight families, twenty or twenty-two people, shared one low house about sixty feet long, its sides and roof made of reed and chestnut bark, with a fire for each family down the middle.

They baked maize bread under hot ashes, kept dogs, fowls and hogs, tended peach trees, and made shoes of deer leather. The families were living on land Jacques Cortelyou had bought from them, people Danckaerts called “the lords thereof.” Cortelyou let them keep a small corner, for which they paid him twenty bushels of maize a year.

Journal of Jasper Danckaerts, 1679–1680 (1913), printed pp. 54–57, entry for September 30, 1679.

Mattano and the move west

As Brooklyn’s land was sold, families camped in small settlements at Gowanus, Nayack and Canarsie. Some followed the Nayack sachem Mattano west to Staten Island and New Jersey. The 1652 agreement that demanded Nayack residents leave is described at Brooklyn’s colonial land claims.

Robert S. Grumet, New World Encounters: Jasper Danckaerts’ View of Indian Life in 17th-Century Brooklyn (Brooklyn: The Brooklyn Historical Society, 1986), exhibition catalog: Brooklyn place identities, archaeology, Danckaerts’ observations, “The Brooklyn Indian Diaspora” and Brooklyn’s Native community.
translation_content:
Recorded forms include Nayack, Naieck, Najeck, Najack, and Nayack-Point. The name is interpreted as a point or corner of land, a meaning also connected with related names such as Noyack.

Why Place Names Matter

“Place-names are also a key part of the shared language through which we come to understand and navigate the world.”

— Words Are Monuments, What's in a Name? (2024), opening discussion

Danckaerts’ 1679 visit shows Nayack families farming, cooking and working on a corner of land they had to rent back from the man who bought it.
whereintheworld_content: The map shows an approximate location for Fort Hamilton at the southwest corner of Brooklyn, not an exact boundary for the older Nayack land or settlement.
